public_rationale: The checkable part is whether the AI proofs reported up to February 2026 were isolated results that do not show broad problem-solving. Terence Tao, who tracked them closely, counted eight problems with meaningful autonomous AI progress as of January 2026, plus six more built on existing literature. He described the successes as coming from the 'long tail' of obscure problems, many with straightforward solutions. He put the true success rate at a point or two, concentrated at the easy end, with no sign that typical problems were within reach. That matches the post's description. AI did make bigger gains later in 2026, including on flagship bounds by September, but that is after the period the claim describes. Whether the results bear on AGI is partly a judgment, but the facts it rests on hold for February 2026.
limitations: The 'do not alter this assessment' part is an evaluative judgment.
The claim is time-bound: later 2026 results were stronger.
The Tao summary page is a living document compiled with AI help, though reviewed by Tao.

statement.excerpt: Reports that language models have produced correct proofs for isolated open problems in mathematics, including specific Erdős problems, do not alter this assessment.
statement.document_title: Rumors of AGI’s arrival have been greatly exaggerated

from_speaker: reports that language models have produced correct proofs
our_interpretation: Plain reading: the LLM proofs of open problems reported up to the post (February 2026) were few and mostly on easier or obscure problems. They did not show broad, domain-general problem-solving that would overturn the judgment that AI falls short of AGI.
The checkable core is how these results were characterized by expert mathematicians tracking them at the time, especially Terence Tao, whom the post cites.
Target period: from late 2025 up to the post date (2026-02-17), when these reports appeared. Later progress is context only.
criteria.support_condition: Expert tallies from the period show AI successes on Erdős problems were a small share, concentrated at the easy or obscure end, often relying on existing literature, and needing human checking.
criteria.contradiction_condition: Expert tallies from the period show AI solving a broad range of hard, central open problems autonomously, including problems typical of the set's difficulty.

evidence.excerpt: Tao conjectured that the scalable nature of AI systems makes them “better suited for being systematically applied to the ‘long tail’ of obscure Erdős problems, many of which actually have straightforward solutions.”
evidence.explanation: Tao described the AI successes as falling on obscure problems that often have straightforward solutions. This matches the post's point that these results do not show deep, general problem-solving.

evidence.excerpt: counting eight different problems where AI models made meaningful autonomous progress on an Erdős problem, with six other cases where progress was made by locating and building on previous research. It’s a long way from AI systems being able to do math without human intervention
evidence.explanation: Only a handful of autonomous successes were recorded at the time, some built on existing literature, and humans were still needed. This supports 'isolated'.

evidence.excerpt: on the Erdős problems, as he measured it in January 2026, the true success rate was only a point or two — non-trivial in absolute count across a thousand-plus problems, but concentrated at the easy end, with no evidence at that point that the median problem was in reach.

evidence.explanation: Tao's January 2026 estimate was a 1-2% success rate, concentrated on easy problems. This backs the claim that the successes were isolated and not evidence of general competence.
